payload.text_html: HVO Kilauea YELLOW/ADVISORY - The Halema'uma'u eruption of Kīlauea remains paused following episode 56 fountaining on November 5. The summit is reinflating and the episode 57 forecast window is November 18-21.
AVO Great Sitkin ORANGE/WATCH - Slow eruption of lava within the summit crater continues; low-level seismicity persists
NMI Ahyi Seamount YELLOW/ADVISORY - Underwater plume detected in satellite data; no significant geophysical signals.

Resuspended ash observed from 1912 eruption. Aviation color code and alert level remain at GREEN/NORMAL.

Strong northwesterly winds in the vicinity of Katmai and the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes have picked up loose volcanic ash erupted during the 1912 Novarupta-Katmai eruption and are carrying it to the southeast. The National Weather Service has issued a SIGMET for this low-level event and suggests that the maximum cloud height is about 6,000 ft (1.8 km) above sea level.

This phenomenon is not the result of recent volcanic activity and occurs during times of high winds and dry snow-free conditions in the Katmai area and other young volcanic areas of Alaska. No eruption is in progress. All of the volcanoes of the Katmai area (Griggs, Katmai, Novarupta, Mageik, Martin, Snowy and Trident) remain at Aviation Color Code GREEN and Alert Level NORMAL. Resuspended volcanic ash should be considered hazardous and could be damaging to aircraft and health.

For more information on volcanic ash and human health, visit the following website: http://volcanoes.usgs.gov/ash/

Official warnings about these ash resuspension events are issued by the National Weather Service: https://www.weather.gov/afc/

Forecasts of airborne ash hazard to aircraft: https://www.weather.gov/aawu/. Volcanic Ash Advisories: https://www.weather.gov/vaac/

Forecasts of ashfall: http://www.weather.gov/afc

Air quality hazards and guidance from Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation, Division of Air Quality: http://dec.alaska.gov/Applications/Air/airtoolsweb/Advisories/Index

Summary: CA volcanoes were at normal background levels of seismicity and deformation during the past week.

Monitored CALIFORNIA VOLCANOES
Current Volcano Alert Level: all NORMAL
Current Aviation Color Code: all GREEN

Activity Update: All volcanoes monitored by CalVO show normal background earthquake activity and deformation. Monitored volcanoes include Mount Shasta, Medicine Lake Volcano, Lassen Volcanic Center, Clear Lake Volcanic Field, Long Valley Volcanic Region, Coso Volcanic Field, Ubehebe Craters, and Salton Buttes.

Past Week Observations for November 02 (0000h PST) to November 08 (2359h PST):

Five earthquakes greater than M1 were recorded within the Clear Lake Volcanic Field, with the largest having a magnitude of M2.8.

Typical seismicity was recorded at The Geysers geothermal field south of the Clear Lake Volcanic Field; 79 earthquakes greater than M1 were recorded, with the largest having a magnitude of M2.7.

Four earthquakes greater than M1 were recorded in the Sierra Nevada Block, south of Mammoth Mountain and Long Valley, with the largest having a magnitude of M1.7.

One earthquake greater than M1 was recorded in the Coso Volcanic Field, with a magnitude of M1.0.

Two earthquakes greater than M1 were recorded near the Salton Buttes, with the largest having a magnitude of M1.3.

Summary: All volcanoes are at normal levels.

Activity Update: All volcanoes in the Cascade Range of Washington and Oregon are at normal background activity levels. These include Mount Baker, Glacier Peak, Mount Rainier, Mount St. Helens, and Mount Adams in Washington State and Mount Hood, Mount Jefferson, Three Sisters, Newberry, and Crater Lake in Oregon.

Over the past week, small earthquakes were detected at Mount St. Helens and Mount Rainier. All monitoring data remain consistent with background activity levels throughout the Cascade Range.

Summary: The Halema'uma'u eruption of Kīlauea remains paused following episode 56 fountaining on November 5. The summit is reinflating and the episode 57 forecast window is November 18-21.

Overview:

The Kīlauea summit eruption within Halema'uma'u is currently paused after episode 56 fountaining ended on November 5. The summit has been steadily reinflating since the end of episode 56, and occasional spatter was visible overnight from both the north and southwest vents. Another fountaining episode remains likely and the current forecast window for episode 57 fountaining is November 18-21.

Summit Observations:

Summit webcams recorded strong glow from both the north and southwest vents overnight. Views from the V1cam livestream webcam overnight showed occasional spatter bursts and flames from both vents.  

Seismic tremor remains elevated during the eruption pause. No earthquakes were located at the summit in the past day.

The Uēkahuna tiltmeter (UWD) has recorded nearly continuous summit inflation since the end of episode 56 lava fountaining. This morning, UWD has recovered a total of about 14 microradians of inflationary tilt since the end of episode 56.

The average sulfur dioxide (SO2) emission rate recorded by the summit gas monitoring array yesterday, November 15, was about 2,000 tonnes per day. Trade winds this morning are carrying volcanic gases to the southwest.

Rift Zone Observations:

Rates of seismicity and ground deformation remain low in the East Rift Zone and Southwest Rift Zone. SO2 emissions from the East Rift Zone remain below the detection limit. 

Analysis:

Following the end of episode 56 on November 5, 2026, summit tiltmeters have recorded a typical post-fountaining recovery, with nearly continuous inflationary tilt at UWD. Based on previous episodes, the ongoing tilt trend, and glow and spatter seen within the eruptive vents, another fountaining episode is likely. The forecast window for episode 57 fountaining is November 18-21. 

Kīlauea has been erupting episodically since December 23, 2024, from two primary vents (north and south) within Halemaʻumaʻu at the summit. Lava fountaining episodes generally last less than 12 hours and are separated by pauses of two or more weeks. 

HVO continues to closely monitor Kīlauea and remains in contact with Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park and the Hawaiʻi County Civil Defense Agency regarding eruptive hazards. 

Summary of episode 56:

  • Lava fountaining occurred between 12:10 p.m. and 6:01 p.m. on November 5, 2026. 
  • Maximum fountain heights were about 660 feet (200 meters). Only the north vent produced fountaining.
  • Tephra fallout was primarily towards the southwest, in closed areas of Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park, with trace amounts on Highway 11.
  • The eruptive plume rose as high as 18,000 feet (5,500 meters) above sea level.
  • Tiltmeter data indicate approximately 8 million cubic yards (6 million cubic meters) of lava were erupted, with an average eruption rate of 260 cubic yards (200 cubic meters) per second.
  • The Uēkahuna tiltmeter (UWD) recorded a total of 17 microradians of deflationary tilt.

Hazards:

Eruptive activity since December 2024 has been occurring within a closed area of Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park. However, recent intrusions highlight that the location of eruptive activity could change. Intrusions can also be hazardous with potential to cause earthquakes, ground cracks, and small landslides. The primary hazards at Kīlauea due to eruptive activity and/or intrusions are:

  • Volcanic Gas: High levels of volcanic gas—primarily water vapor (H2O), carbon dioxide (CO2), and sulfur dioxide (SO2)—are continually released during an eruption. Emissions can remain locally hazardous in the areas immediately downwind of the vents, even when the vents are not actively erupting. SO2 reacts in the atmosphere to create vog (volcanic air pollution) downwind. SO2 and vog may cause respiratory and other problems at high concentrations. Further information on vog can be found at https://vog.ivhhn.org/
  • Tephra: Small glassy volcanic fragments—volcanic ash, pumice, scoria, Pele’s hair and reticulite—are created by the lava fountains. A combination of fountaining dynamics and wind conditions determines where tephra fall may occur for any given eruption episode. Larger particles fall near the vents while light particles may be wafted greater distances. These particles may be remobilized during windy conditions following recent eruptive episodes. Residents and visitors should minimize exposure to these fragments, which can cause skin, eye, and respiratory irritation. More information and guidance on tephra fall hazards is available at https://seagrant.soest.hawaii.edu/resource-and-guidance-for-volcanic-tephra-fall/ and https://vog.ivhhn.org/sites/default/files/PelesHair_FAQs_v2.pdf 
  • Lava flows: Hawaiian lava flows generally advance slowly downslope but destroy everything in their paths. Lava flows that erupt within Halemaʻumaʻu remain confined to the crater, including those during the eruption that started in December 2024. However, intrusive activity could result in lava flows outside of Halemaʻumaʻu. Hazards associated with active or recent lava flows include hot and glassy (sharp) surfaces that can cause serious burns, abrasions, and lacerations upon contact with unprotected or exposed skin; uneven and rough terrain can lead to falls and other injuries; hot temperatures that can cause heat exhaustion or dehydration, or in heavy rain can produce steamy ground-fog that can be acidic, severely limiting visibility and sometimes causing difficulty breathing.
  • Earthquakes and ground cracks: Shallow magma movement and eruptions can produce minor to severe ground fractures and subsidence features. These ground cracks can continue to widen and offset as magma migration continues, may have unstable overhanging edges, and should be avoided. Other significant hazards exist around Kīlauea caldera from Halemaʻumaʻu crater wall instability, ground cracking, and rockfalls that can be enhanced by earthquakes.

Additionally, close to the eruptive vents, the tephra material on the crater rim is prone to cracking, slumping, and small landslides that sometimes expose hot and molten material within. This underscores the extremely hazardous nature of Kīlauea's caldera rim surrounding Halemaʻumaʻu crater, an area that has been closed to the public since early 2008.

Summary: Underwater plume detected in satellite data; no significant geophysical signals.

A plume of discolored water was visible in a partially cloudy satellite image over Ahyi Seamount on November 10. No notable activity was detected in distal geophysical monitoring data. 

Eruptive activity at Ahyi seamount may present a hazard to mariners in the water above and near the volcano. The summit has shallowed over the course of previous eruptions to 180 feet (55 m) below sea level, but the lack of local real-time data means we are unable to forecast or warn of impending eruptions. We will continue to monitor satellite and distal hydroacoustic data for additional evidence for, or escalation of, volcanic activity.

Summary: YVO Monthly Update: background seismicity and deformation

Yellowstone Caldera activity remains at background levels, with 66 located earthquakes in October (largest = M2.0). Deformation measurements indicate no significant uplift or subsidence of the caldera or north caldera rim for the past several months. Giant Geyser, in Upper Geyser Basin, erupted three times in October.

 

Recent Work and News

Hydrothermal activity in Yellowstone National Park during the month of October included an eruption of Echinus Geyser (Norris Geyser Basin) on October 26.  Giant Geyser (Upper Geyser Basin)—the second tallest geyser in the park—erupted on October 5, 13, and 22.  In addition, the small pool of hot water that formed via collapse in Biscuit Basin after the June 13, 2026, hydrothermal explosion had at least two small eruptions.  Steamboat Geyser, in Norris Geyser Basin, was characterized by minor eruptions and has only had one major eruption thus far in 2026.

 

Seismicity

During October 2026, the University of Utah Seismograph Stations, responsible for the operation and analysis of the Yellowstone Seismic Network, located 66 earthquakes in the Yellowstone National Park region. The largest event of the month was a micro earthquake of magnitude 2.0 located about 15 miles south of West Thumb, Yellowstone National Park, on October 4 at 5:32 p.m. MDT.

There were no swarms identified during October.

Earthquake activity in Yellowstone is at background levels.

 

Ground Deformation

Data from continuous GPS stations indicate little net deformation of the caldera or north caldera regions over the past several months.  Subtle variations in ground motion are probably caused by seasonal changes, especially in groundwater conditions.

An example of GPS data can be found at http://www.unavco.org/instrumentation/networks/status/pbo/data/NRWY (click on Static Plots / Cleaned)
